title: The Hollow
mood: Night after night in the dark, Vexana fits salvaged plates together, until something stands up.

hero.alt: In the dark, a glowing gold crest, a cross over a crescent, rises above the head of a tall unlit shape, with violet star-shaped plates on either side.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 44

segs.t: Vexana laid the plates out in the dark, one beside the next. A knee and a shoulder from the first sack. The other knee and a thigh from the second. Two forearms and a hip from the third.
She pushed back her right sleeve. The star at her wrist gave just enough light for her hands.
No Ender comes here,
she thought.
Nothing sees.
On a feeder run she had taken a hammer and an iron bar from a dead workshop. Her father’s screwdriver lay in a toolbox in her room, across the city. The hammer and the bar would have to do.
She had no bolts and no drill. But Ender plates had edges made to catch on one another. That was how an Ender’s joints held. She tried each edge against the next. Most would not catch.
When two came close, she beat the edges with the hammer until they did. The blows did not echo. She felt every one in her wrists.
The knee took longest. It slid off the thigh twice. The third time it caught.
“Hold,” she told it.
It held. She took her hands away slowly.
“There.”
She heard herself. Guinevere talked to her drones like that, all through training. Vexana had always thought it was silly.
She picked up the next plate and set its edge to the hip.
“Stay,” she told it.
Later she held out her hand for the bar without looking. Nothing came into it.
She had learned that in a gun pit on the city wall. Her father would hold out his hand without looking, and she would put the right tool in it. He never had to say which.
She looked at her own open hand. Then she reached over and picked up the bar herself.
Each errand night she carried one more sack home, paid for in places. A suit needed a core at its heart, so she had asked for cores too.
“Cores cost extra,” Selena had said. “Three places each.”
Whenever she looked up from the work, the crack of sky was wider. It no longer hid behind her thumb. When it went pale with dawn, she scratched a line on the iron bar.
A door let her out onto cinders and rusted track, far from the dome.
“The rail yards north of the dome. Dusk.” That had been the order, out of the cold point under her breastbone.
The feeders came through behind her. They spread out over a fallen crane and began to tear at it.
The sky over the dead ground was still pale. If the lines on her bar were right, it was her birthday.
Far off, along the foot of the dome, ran the dark line of the city wall. Somewhere in its shadow stood the Shield houses where she had lived with her father.
On her birthdays he had taken her up the wall stair to look out over this ground. He named the bright stars after guns. One small one, low over the dark ground, he gave to her.
“It comes out first,” he had said. “Before it’s even dark.”
From the yard of the Shield’s home she had never found it again. The barracks roofs were in the way.
She looked away from the wall, out over the open dark.
It was there. Small and low, the only one yet.
“Still first,” she told it.
Behind her the feeders tore at the crane. None of them looked up.
One night the sack she carried home held a core, as big as two fists, dark and cracked across.
She fitted it into the chest. She closed the last plate over it and stood back.
The machine stood over her, taller than the star’s light could reach. She had to lift her wrist to see its head.

Its plate was dark purple, edged in gold, off some kind of Ender she had never fought. A golden crest rose above its head, a cross over a crescent. She had beaten the chest plate, magenta, to fit around the core. Only now did she see the shape. A heart.
She left it.
Behind the heart, beside the core, she had made room for one person. Her own size.
It was as dead as the empty suit in the ditch.
If it stays dark,
she thought,
I’ve built a statue.
Then she would have to reach the Mother Matrix on her own wings, and get there with less to give it.
She laid her palm on its chest, over the heart.
For a long moment it stayed dark. Under her glove the plate gave nothing back. The cold point under her breastbone waited. She left it alone.
She thought of a street at the dome’s foot, and Guinevere’s hand closing on hers as Vexana pulled her to her feet. Guinevere had held on.
She thought of the lamp at the top of the Academy’s tower, and the long shape in it turning along the sky. Searching it for her, one piece at a time.
Under her palm, deep in the chest, something began to hum.
The eyes lit. Yellow, like the rings of Guinevere’s drones.
The heart blazed magenta.
Nothing in the dark had ordered it. At her wrist, the star burned brighter.
“In the dark of night, I awaken the Aspirant dawn,” Vexana said.
Lit and humming, the machine stood over her. It did not move.
She took her palm from its chest and held out her hand.
Its great hand rose with hers, and stopped when hers stopped.
Mine,
she thought.
It answers to me.
Guinevere would have said something to it. So Vexana did.
“Let us go together, to protect her.”
The hum went on in the dark.
The hollow. The last weeks.
Three giants stood behind the first one now.

Every sack since then had gone into them. She had not fitted them as carefully. They only had to stand and strike. One had a gray shoulder on a purple arm. Each held a sword of Ender blade, fitted length by length, longer than a house.
Three more cracked cores had come, at three places each. She had woken each giant the same way, with her palm on its chest, thinking of Guinevere.
The first time she slept among them, she woke to dark. Four shapes stood over her, their eyes dark.
Her hand went to her staff. Then she laid her other palm on the first one’s chest. Its eyes lit. The giants’ eyes lit after it.
They ran on her power. While she slept, none of it reached them.
She tested it. When she held a charged shot in the staff, all four pairs of eyes dimmed. When she let it go, they came back.
In a hard fight I’ll have less to give them,
she thought.
Remember that.
She climbed into the first one. The heart closed in front of her. She saw the hollow through its yellow eyes, from far above where she sat.
This one carries me up,
she thought.
When the Matrix opens its chest.
She climbed out again and stood among the four of them. She needed a word for them.
Once a soldier had brought her father’s toolbox to the home and set it by her cot. “That Ender never got past him,” he had said. “Not while he stood.”
Her father had stood until he fell.
Guards,
she thought. They would stand over Guinevere when she could not.
She did not mean to come back down from the Matrix. After she was gone, they would still be standing.
“Eternal Guards,” she said.
“The edge of the dome. Before dawn.”
It was the old order, out of the cold point. Her Guards did not stir.
She turned to where the door would open. Far off, past the vast bulk of the Mother Matrix, something moved.
Nothing that far out had ever moved before.
A storm was turning in the dark, slow and violet. Lightning ran through it. Each flash lit something huge hung inside it, all black blades.

She had seen that shape once, on a screen, with Guinevere beside her. Joe’s last slide in the lesson on weak spots: a shaking recording from the Academy’s oldest records. A ship of black blades over a city in a red sky.
The Storm Citadel.
She let her Guards’ eyes go dark, one after another. Then she pulled her sleeve down over the star.
